title: The Augsburg Confession (Condensed)
subtitle: The chief articles of faith from the Augsburg Confession of 1530, faithfully condensed, the founding confession of the Lutheran Reformation, with notes.
intro:
On June 25, 1530, before the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg, a group of German princes and city representatives stood and had read aloud, in German, a confession of what was being taught in their churches. Luther, still under imperial ban, could not attend. The document was drafted by Philip Melanchthon, his careful colleague. The signers were laymen risking their lands and their lives. They signed anyway. The Augsburg Confession became the founding charter of Lutheranism and the model for nearly every Protestant confession after it.

Its tone surprises people. It is not a manifesto. Melanchthon wrote to show that the reformers taught nothing contrary to Scripture or the catholic church of the creeds, and that Rome, not Wittenberg, had introduced the novelties. The center is Article IV: we are justified freely, for Christ's sake, through faith, and not by our own works or merits. Everything else in the document orbits that claim.

What follows is a faithful condensation of the doctrinal articles of Part One (Articles I–XXI), not the full text. Each article is summarized in close paraphrase. The complete confession, with its second part on abuses that had been corrected, runs much longer and rewards a full reading. Even condensed, the shape is visible: a church trying to prove it was not inventing a new faith but recovering an old one. That is what reformation means, when it is honest.
text:
The following is a condensed summary of the twenty-one doctrinal articles of Part One. It is a faithful paraphrase, not the full text.

Article I. Of God. The churches teach, with the Council of Nicaea, that there is one divine essence, God, eternal, without body, of infinite power, wisdom, and goodness; and yet three Persons of the same essence and power, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. They condemn the old heresies against this, including the Arians and Mohammedans, and the new teachers who deny the Trinity.

Article II. Of Original Sin. Since the fall of Adam, all who are naturally born are conceived and born in sin, without the fear of God, without trust in God, and with concupiscence. This disease of origin is truly sin, condemning and bringing eternal death upon those not born again through baptism and the Holy Ghost. The Pelagians are condemned, who deny that original depravity is sin.

Article III. Of the Son of God. The Word, the Son of God, took human nature in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, so that there are two natures, divine and human, inseparably joined in one Person, one Christ, true God and true man; who was truly born, suffered, was crucified, dead, and buried, that he might reconcile the Father to us and be a sacrifice not only for original guilt but for all actual sins of men. He rose, ascended, reigns, and will return to judge, as the Apostles' Creed declares.

Article IV. Of Justification. Men cannot be justified before God by their own strength, merits, or works, but are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, when they believe that they are received into favor and their sins forgiven for Christ's sake, who by his death made satisfaction for our sins. This faith God imputes for righteousness in his sight.

Article V. Of the Ministry. That we may obtain this faith, the ministry of teaching the Gospel and administering the Sacraments was instituted. Through the Word and Sacraments, as through instruments, the Holy Ghost is given, who works faith, where and when it pleases God, in those who hear the Gospel. They condemn those who think the Holy Ghost comes to men without the external Word, through their own preparations and works.

Article VI. Of New Obedience. This faith is bound to bring forth good fruits, and it is necessary to do the good works commanded by God, because of God's will, but not that we should rely on those works to merit justification before God. For remission of sins and justification is apprehended by faith.

Article VII. Of the Church. One holy Church is to continue forever. The Church is the congregation of saints in which the Gospel is rightly taught and the Sacraments rightly administered. For the true unity of the Church it is enough to agree concerning the doctrine of the Gospel and the administration of the Sacraments; it is not necessary that human traditions, rites, or ceremonies be everywhere alike.

Article VIII. What the Church Is. Although the Church is properly the congregation of saints and true believers, yet since in this life many hypocrites and evil persons are mingled with them, it is lawful to use Sacraments administered by evil men. Both the Sacraments and the Word are effectual by reason of the institution and commandment of Christ, even when delivered by evil men.

Article IX. Of Baptism. Baptism is necessary to salvation, and through baptism the grace of God is offered. Children are to be baptized, who, being offered to God through baptism, are received into God's grace. The Anabaptists are condemned, who reject the baptism of children.

Article X. Of the Lord's Supper. The body and blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat the Supper of the Lord. Those who teach otherwise are rejected.

Article XI. Of Confession. Private absolution ought to be retained in the churches, although in confession an enumeration of all sins is not necessary, for it is impossible, 'Who can understand his errors?' (Psalm 19:12).

Article XII. Of Repentance. For those who have fallen after baptism, remission of sins may be obtained whenever they are converted. Repentance consists of two parts: contrition, the terrors smiting the conscience through the knowledge of sin; and faith, born of the Gospel, which believes that for Christ's sake sins are forgiven, comforts the conscience, and delivers it from terrors. Then good works, the fruits of repentance, are bound to follow.

Article XIII. Of the Use of the Sacraments. The Sacraments were ordained not only to be marks of profession among men, but rather to be signs and testimonies of God's will toward us, instituted to awaken and confirm faith in those who use them. They are to be used with faith that believes the promises offered and set forth through them.

Article XIV. Of Ecclesiastical Order. No one should publicly teach in the Church or administer the Sacraments unless he be regularly called.

Article XV. Of Ecclesiastical Usages. Those usages are to be kept which may be kept without sin and which serve peace and good order in the Church, such as holy days and festivals. Yet consciences are not to be burdened as though such observance were necessary to salvation. Human traditions instituted to propitiate God, to merit grace, and to make satisfaction for sins are contrary to the Gospel.

Article XVI. Of Civil Affairs. Lawful civil ordinances are good works of God. Christians may lawfully hold civil office, sit as judges, wage just wars, serve as soldiers, make legal contracts, hold property, take oaths when required by magistrates, marry, and be given in marriage. The Gospel does not destroy the State or the family, but requires that they be kept as ordinances of God, and that charity be exercised in such ordinances. Christians must obey their magistrates and laws, except when commanded to sin; then they ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Article XVII. Of Christ's Return to Judgment. At the consummation of the world Christ will appear for judgment and will raise up all the dead. He will give to the godly eternal life and everlasting joys, but ungodly men and the devils he will condemn to be tormented without end. Condemned are those who think there will be an end to the punishments of the damned, and those who scatter the opinion that before the resurrection the godly shall take possession of the kingdoms of this world, the wicked being everywhere suppressed.

Article XVIII. Of Free Will. Man's will has some liberty to choose civil righteousness and to work things subject to reason. But it has no power, without the Holy Ghost, to work the righteousness of God, that is, spiritual righteousness, since the natural man receives not the things of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14). This righteousness is wrought in the heart when the Holy Ghost is received through the Word.

Article XIX. Of the Cause of Sin. Although God creates and preserves nature, the cause of sin is the will of the wicked, of the devil and ungodly men, which, God not aiding, turns itself from God.

Article XX. Of Good Works. Our teachers are falsely accused of forbidding good works. Their writings on the commandments show they have given useful instruction concerning all estates and duties of life. But works do not reconcile us to God or merit forgiveness of sins; this is received by faith alone, for Christ's sake. Whoever trusts to merit grace by works despises the merit and grace of Christ. Yet faith is bound to bring forth good fruits, and we must do the good works commanded by God, because it is God's will, not in order to be justified by them. Faith is not merely knowledge of history, but trust which receives the promise of grace and of righteousness.

Article XXI. Of the Worship of the Saints. The memory of the saints may be set before us, that we may follow their faith and good works according to our calling. But Scripture teaches not the invocation of saints, nor to ask help of saints, since it sets before us the one Christ as Mediator, Propitiation, High Priest, and Intercessor (1 Timothy 2:5; 1 John 2:1).

This is about the sum of doctrine taught in our churches, in which nothing can be discerned that differs from the Scriptures, or from the Church Catholic, or from the Church of Rome as known from its writers. The whole dissension concerns certain abuses which have crept into the churches without rightful authority, and those are treated in the Confession's second part.

annotations.phrase: freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith
annotations.note: Article IV is the article by which, the Lutherans later said, the church stands or falls. Justification is a verdict received, not a wage earned. Everything distinctively Protestant flows from this sentence.

annotations.phrase: This disease of origin is truly sin
annotations.note: Against the medieval drift toward treating fallen desire as mere weakness, Article II insists the inherited condition itself is sin, not just the acts it produces. The depth of the diagnosis is what makes grace necessary rather than helpful.

annotations.phrase: where and when it pleases God
annotations.note: Faith is the Spirit's work through the preached Word and the Sacraments, not a product of technique. Article V quietly rules out both manufactured revival and a private spirituality that bypasses the gathered church.

annotations.phrase: it is not necessary that human traditions, rites, or ceremonies be everywhere alike
annotations.note: Article VII defines the church by Gospel and Sacraments, not by uniform customs, a deliberately minimal definition that made room for reform without claiming to start a new church.

annotations.phrase: it is lawful to use Sacraments administered by evil men
annotations.note: An old answer (against the Donatists) to a permanent anxiety: the power of Word and Sacrament rests on Christ's institution, not the minister's character. Your baptism does not become invalid when your pastor falls.

annotations.phrase: The body and blood of Christ are truly present
annotations.note: Article X marks the line between Lutherans and the Swiss reformers, who read the Supper as memorial. Melanchthon states real presence without explaining its mode. Deliberately less than Rome's transubstantiation, more than Zurich's remembrance.

annotations.phrase: contrition, the terrors smiting the conscience
annotations.note: Repentance in Augsburg is not self-improvement. It is being genuinely afraid of what you have done, and then being given, from outside yourself, a promise strong enough to quiet the fear. Law, then Gospel. The order is the pastoral method of the whole Reformation.
Article XIV: the Reformation was not a free-for-all. Public ministry requires a public call from the church. Private judgment about doctrine never licensed private seizure of the pulpit.

annotations.phrase: Christians may lawfully hold civil office
annotations.note: Against radical groups who withdrew from civic life, Article XVI affirms ordinary vocations (judge, soldier, spouse, property-holder) as good works of God. Holiness does not require leaving the world. It requires serving in it.

Article XXI honors the saints as examples and refuses them as intercessors. The issue is not respect for the dead but the sufficiency of the living Christ. There is no waiting room between the believer and God.
